svg.title: OSPF area types, which LSAs each admits, and the decision path for choosing one
svg.desc: Six rows: backbone area 0 admits every LSA type and must stay contiguous; normal area admits everything; stub area refuses Type 5 external routes and uses a default route instead, admitting types 1, 2 and 3; totally stub admits only types 1 and 2 and is the common spoke optimisation; NSSA refuses Type 5 but allows Type 7 so the site can still import local external routes; totally NSSA additionally refuses Type 3. A right-hand decision box walks through the choice: does the site need to know external detail, no means stub or totally stub, yes means NSSA or totally NSSA, and then does it need other areas' detail, no means take the totally variant. A warning strip lists three hard constraints: the area cannot be area 0, it cannot contain an ASBR, and every router in the area must be configured identically or no adjacency forms.
svg.text: Area types are filters, and the filter is defined by which LSAs are admitted
Pick the area type from the number of exits at the site — not from which one shrinks the table the most
AREA TYPE
ADMITS
WHERE IT FITS
Backbone (area 0)
must be contiguous
all types
carries every inter-area path
Normal area
all types
ordinary office and data centre areas
Stub
branch and edge sites, one exit only
Totally stub
spoke sites — the most common optimisation
NSSA
edge sites that must import local externals
Totally NSSA
edge site with a local exit and a small table
HOW TO CHOOSE, IN TWO QUESTIONS
Does this site need the detail of external routes?
No — everything exits
through headquarters
→ Stub / Totally Stub
Yes — local Internet
exit or local externals
→ NSSA / Totally NSSA
And then: does it need other areas' detail?
No → take the Totally variant (smallest table).
Yes → plain Stub or plain NSSA.
Three hard constraints on a stub area
1. It cannot be area 0.
2. It cannot contain an ASBR, so redistribution is silently ignored.
3. Every router in the area must be configured as stub, or no adjacency forms.
The silent failure to test for: a site with a local Internet backup is configured as stub. redistribute static is accepted on the
command line and ignored by the process, so the backup default route never enters OSPF. The routing table shrinks, acceptance passes,
and the site goes dark the first time the primary link fails. Test the failure, not the configuration line.
Rule that prevents the whole class of problem: the area type must match the number of exits at the site. One exit → stub. More than one exit,
including a local Internet path → NSSA. Every redundancy design needs its own fault-injection case, tested with the primary link down.
Also verify what actually landed in the table, because a redistributed route that is silently dropped looks exactly like a route that was never needed.
